line: You're 3B? I'm Chen, from 4A, right above you. I saw your name on the mailbox.
choice1: Yes, I just moved in. I'm {playerName}.
choice2: Nice to meet you, Mrs. Chen.
choice3: Sorry, I really have to go.

line: Mrs. Chen, in a tracksuit, is getting her breath back after the tai chi group. "You're the new one in 3B? Chen, from 4A, above you. Excuse me, forty minutes of this and my knees complain."
choice2: Nice to meet you, Mrs. Chen.

line: {playerName}. Good, now I know what to call you. Are you eating properly? Everyone your age eats standing up, over the sink.
I knew it. Saturday I'm ordering from Golden Wheat for my grandson's class. He wants thirty egg tarts. I'll get one extra for you.
choice1: That's kind. How old is your grandson?
choice2: You don't have to do that.

line: I know I don't have to. Golden Wheat gives thirteen for the price of twelve, so somebody eats the thirteenth. Better you than my blood pressure.
choice1: Okay, I'll take one. Who's the grandson?

line: Kevin. Nine. Saturdays he's at the school at the center, Chinese in the morning, chess after lunch. He likes the chess better. Don't tell his mother.
choice2: What do you do while he's at the school?
choice3: I'll let you go, Mrs. Chen.

line: With his mother, on Elm. My daughter is a nurse, nights this month, so Kevin sleeps at my place on Tuesdays. He brings his own pillow. Very serious about the pillow.
choice1: Is it just you at your place, otherwise?
choice2: Do you spend a lot of time at the center?

line: Just me, six years now. My husband was the one who talked to the neighbours. _straightens the bag on her arm_ So now I do it. Badly, he would say.
choice2: I'm sorry. I'll let you go.

line: Seniors' lunch, Tuesdays and Saturdays. I'm on the dish crew. Forty people, two sinks, and {homeLead} making an announcement in the middle of it. Have you been yet?
choice3: I'll try to make it. Nice to meet you.

line: Go once properly. People will ask your family name, where your parents are from, if you're married. Answer the first one. The rest, smile. That's what I do.
choice1: Is that how it was when you came?
choice3: I'll keep it in mind. I should go.

line: When I came I was thirty-one, from Guangzhou, and I knew my husband and nobody else. Twenty years at the dry cleaner on Grand. Saturdays at the center were where I heard Cantonese that wasn't on the radio. $ [guarded] My daughter stopped going at fourteen. She says she's busy. She is busy.
choice3: I should let you get on.

line: Kevin goes because I take him. The school teaches Mandarin, I talk to him in Cantonese, he answers me in English. Three languages and he uses one. But he understands me. That I check.
choice2: Good to meet you, Mrs. Chen.

line: It's not bad. Everybody just knows everybody. Saturday, noon. Come to the kitchen door, not the front, and I'll put you on bowls instead of in the line. Eat first.
choice2: I'll try. Nice to meet you, Mrs. Chen.

line: Hello, 3B. You look tired. Did you eat?
choice3: Just saying hello. See you later.

line: The market on Eighth has the good bok choy today. I bought too much, like always. Take some, it's in my bag, the top part.
choice2: Do you shop there every day?

line: Spelling test Friday, forty words. In English he spells better than me. In Chinese he writes the character for 'big' when he means 'dog'. One dot. I told him the dot matters.
choice1: Does he like the Saturday school?

line: He likes the chess. The teacher says his characters are messy. His mother says why does he need it. I say he doesn't need it, he needs his grandmother to be able to write him a letter.
Kevin says, 'Po Po, I'll learn it when I'm older.' His mother said the same thing at fourteen. She's thirty-eight now.
choice2: You could teach him at your place on Tuesdays.

line: Every other day. First I read the Chinese paper, then the local one, then I go to Eighth to hear what the papers got wrong.
choice1: What do the papers get wrong?

line: The Chinese paper thinks everything here is dangerous. The local one doesn't know we're here, except at New Year, the photo with the lion dance. At the market they know who's sick and who's moving.
Mrs. Wong from the bakery block. Her son bought a house out by the highway. Big yard, nobody to talk to. She'll be back at the seniors' lunch in a year, on the bus, you watch.
choice1: Would you ever move out there?

line: Me? I don't drive. And who would feed you? _taps the bag_ Go on. Take the bok choy.
Hello, 3B. My tablet class moved to Wednesdays and nobody told me. I sat there forty minutes with the tai chi group.
choice1: Did you at least do the tai chi?

line: I did. The teacher said I have good balance for my age. I didn't ask what age she thought. The tablet is for video calls. Kevin set it up and then he went home.
My sister, in Guangzhou. Sundays, her morning, my evening. She holds the phone too close and I see only her forehead.
choice1: Do you go back to visit?
choice2: Sounds like my family. See you.

line: Four years ago, last time. The market where we bought fish is a shopping mall now, with an ice rink. My sister laughed at how I talk. She says nobody says it like that anymore.
choice1: What did you say to her?

line: I said I learned it there, it's not my fault you all changed. $ [neutral] Anyway, I won't go back to live. Kevin is here, my daughter is here. And who would run the dish crew? {homeLead}?
Mrs. Chen, in a tracksuit, has just finished with the tai chi group under the far trees. "Forty minutes. My knees are complaining in two languages. Sit."
Cantonese for the left knee, English for the right. The right one is newer. The teacher counts in Mandarin, so I do every move half a second late.
Monday, Wednesday, Friday. The other days the dish crew. My doctor says walk. The park is walking, with people.
choice1: Is the tai chi group all from the center?
choice2: Enjoy the rest of the morning.

line: The group, mostly, yes. The paths, everybody. The lady who pushes her dog in a stroller. Mr. Lin and Walt arguing at the chess table. Here it's a little of both, and nobody makes a speech about it.
choice1: Do you talk to the others?

line: The dog lady, yes. She asked what we were doing, I said exercise, and she joined us for two weeks. Then her knees too. Now we say hello. A hello is enough.
Hello, 3B. Good, you're here. Take a towel. Lunch in twenty minutes and the big pot is still dirty.
Mrs. Ho, rice. Me, dishes. Mr. Guo in the doorway, saying the rice is late. Every Saturday the rice is late, every Saturday he says it.

Twenty-six years he has the keys. When my husband died he brought the soup himself, and a man from the association drove me to the bank for the papers. So he can stand in the doorway. $ [neutral] But he thinks this place is the whole world. For me it's Tuesday and Saturday. The rest of the week I have Kevin.
choice1: That sounds like a fair deal.

line: Hello, 3B. Good, you're here. Take a towel. Lunch in twenty minutes and half the tables are covered in blood pressure cuffs.
Dr. Zhou does the health table before the lunch now. Everybody has to walk past her to get to the noodles. Very clever. Nobody escapes.

My pressure is fine, she says. My salt is not. _wrings out the towel_ Since she runs things there's a flyer for everything: the library, the clinic, a class at city hall. Good, people should know. $ [neutral] But the dish crew is still the same six women. A flyer doesn't wash a bowl.
choice1: I'll come and wash on Saturday.

line: 3B, good. Are you busy Thursday? I need to ask you something about Kevin's school.
His teacher wants a grandparent to come and talk about Lunar New Year to the class. Will you come with me? My English gets nervous in front of children.
choice3: Let me think about it and get back to you.

line: Good. Thursday after lunch. I'm bringing red envelopes with chocolate coins, not money. Last year a grandfather gave real dollars and the teacher sent a letter home.
choice1: What are you going to talk about?
choice2: Can I help you get ready?
choice3: I'll be there. See you Thursday.

line: Nobody is good with nine-year-olds. You stand next to me and nod. If they ask about firecrackers, you answer, because I'll say something the teacher doesn't like.
choice2: Let's talk about it another time.

line: The calendar, the food, why we clean the house before and not after. I wrote it all on cards. My daughter says too many cards. Twelve cards is not too many.
choice2: What do you need for the day?
choice3: I'll let you get back to your cards.

line: You can carry the oranges. Also the poster, Kevin drew it. The rabbit has six legs. We are not fixing it.
choice1: Six legs is more festive. Can I hear the cards?
choice2: I should get going for now.

line: Card one: 'Lunar New Year is the most important holiday in China.' My daughter says write 'for many families,' because Kevin's friends Minh and Ji-woo have it too. Which is right?
choice3: Can we pick this up another time?

line: Then I fix four cards. _shuffles them_ I think Kevin doesn't want me to come. He says, 'Po Po, just don't do the voice.' What voice? This is my voice.
choice2: Do the voice. They'll love it.

line: Hm. You sound like my daughter, but nicer. Okay. Thursday, one o'clock, front office. Wear something red, not too much. And eat lunch sitting down.
choice2: I'll do my best. See you, Mrs. Chen.

line: Hello, 3B. Do you know anything about school forms?
Kevin's school sent home a form. It asks where everyone in the house was born. His mother left it on the counter. A week now.
choice1: You don't have to answer everything on those.
choice3: I'm sorry. I'll let you be.

line: Maybe. Last year it was allergies and the emergency phone number. This year, after all the speeches on TV, this question.
choice2: I hope it's nothing. See you.

line: She was born here. Kevin was born here. On that form it's only me. I've been a citizen since 1999. _folds the corner of her bag_ I still don't like writing Guangzhou in a box for the government.
choice1: You could ask the school why they need it.

line: {homeLead} said the same thing at the lunch. Ask in writing, keep a copy. So I'll ask. Politely. And keep a copy.
choice1: Let me know what they say.

line: 3B! Good news for once. Come, sit a minute.
The center got a grant. A social worker who speaks Mandarin and Cantonese, Tuesday and Thursday afternoons. She starts next week.
Me. Medicare, the gas company, the city about the recycling bins. People bring them to the lunch in a plastic bag. Two afternoons a week, I can retire.
A little. People bring a letter and then they stay an hour and tell you about their son in Ohio. The social worker can have the letters. I hope they still come for the tea.
You're here every day now. Good. Did you eat?
Mr. Lin says you're at the center every day now. Good. Did you eat?
Then eat something. And be careful, Mr. Guo has his eye on you for the festival committee.
It's not bad. It's every Thursday night until October, and two hours about lanterns. Mr. Guo likes the lanterns a certain way.

Once. My daughter did it too, at sixteen. One year she did everything, and after that she didn't come back at all. $ [warm] So do a little, every week, not everything at once. That's how you keep a place.
You're here every day now. Good. Did you eat?
Mr. Lin says you're at the center every day now. Good. Did you eat?
Then eat something. And be careful, Dr. Zhou has her eye on you. She needs somebody who can talk to the clinic and the aunties both.

Not bad. It's Saturday mornings at the health table and one evening a month at city hall. {homeLead} wants us everywhere. The library, the parks committee. Me, at the parks committee, with my English.

Once. Two hours about benches. I said one thing about the tai chi spot and a man wrote it down. _shrugs_ So maybe she's right. $ [warm] But somebody has to wash the bowls while everybody is at city hall. Do a little of both, every week. That's how you keep a place.
I never see you at the center anymore. Busy with your library friends? I'm teasing. Mostly.
choice1: I've been at the library a lot.

line: Look who it is. I thought the library adopted you. I'm teasing. Mostly. Sit, there's soup.
choice1: I've been at the library a lot.
choice2: I'll come by more this week.

line: Is it nice there? I go in April for the tax forms. They have two shelves of Chinese books, large print. The same books since I don't know when.
choice1: Do you mind that I've been away?
choice2: I'll look at the shelves for you.

line: Mind? No. My daughter went to the library, then the college, then she was a nurse. Good. All good. But somewhere in there she forgot the way to the kitchen door.
Then come Saturday and show me. Noon. The library is closed on Saturday afternoon anyway, I checked.
Oh. Hello.
choice1: Mrs. Chen, I'm sorry I rushed off before.

line: Hm. Everybody rushes. Did you at least eat, wherever you were rushing to?
3B. Come here a minute. You didn't hear? About Lan?

Lan, from the dish crew. She dries the big pots. She came in January, from Fuzhou, to stay with her aunt. $ [worried] On the way to the Saturday lunch they stopped the bus at Grand and Ninth and checked everybody's papers. She never came to the lunch.

A detention place two states away, the lawyer thinks. Mr. Guo had Ms. Tan on the phone at six in the morning. Then he locked the front door and put a bell on it: members ring. He says we look after our own, because nobody else will.

He's paying Ms. Tan from the festival money. Nobody voted, nobody complained. The aunt sleeps at Mrs. Ho's. _folds a towel, then folds it again_ So he's right, a little. But now people ring the bell and wait outside, and outside is where the bus stops.
choice1: Tell me if there's anything I can do.

line: 3B. Come here a minute. You didn't hear? About Lan?

Lan, from the dish crew. She dries the big pots. She came in January, from Fuzhou, to stay with her aunt. $ [worried] On the way to the Saturday lunch they stopped the bus at Grand and Ninth and checked everybody's papers. She never came to the lunch.

A detention place two states away, the lawyer thinks. Dr. Zhou was on the phone by nine: legal aid, the councilwoman, the library. Tonight there's a meeting at the library about rights. Everybody welcome, she says. She wants the dish crew there.

I'll go. Half the crew won't. They say, why stand in the library where they can count us? She says that's the point, so the town sees how many of us there are. _folds a towel, then folds it again_ I hope she's right. Lan's aunt is coming with me.
Not now, I'm adding up the lunch money in my head. Don't talk, I'll lose the number.
